1._section_summary: This section discusses self-compassion as a within-persons protective factor in relation to body image and eating behaviors. It reviews two key daily diary studies: Study 1 (Breines et al. 2014) with college women over four days, and Study 2 (Kelly & Stephen 2016) with college women over seven days. Both studies found that when participants experienced higher-than-usual self-compassion, they reported better body image outcomes and more adaptive eating behaviors, suggesting that fluctuations in self-compassion within individuals are associated with variability in body image and eating experiences.

4._section_summary: This Discussion section presents findings from a single study examining how self-compassion buffers the relationship between daily interactions with body-focused others and body image/eating outcomes among college women. The study employed a within-persons and between-persons design, revealing that higher-than-usual self-compassion on specific days protected against negative effects of body-focused interactions, and that women with higher overall self-compassion were less negatively affected by frequent interactions with body-focused others. The findings suggest that self-compassion may be particularly protective against diet- and body-focused talk, but less critical when exposure involves exercise-focused interactions.
